newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish government details 1997 borrowing plans.
newsitem.headline: Finnish government details 1997 borrowing plans.

text.p: The Finnish government said it had sought authorisation for 77 billion markka of long-term gross borrowing and for a 55 billion markka ceiling on short-term state debt in 1997.

The state budget put the 1997 deficit at 28.10 billion markka, but the government sought authorisation from parliament for 31 billion markka of net borrowing and said long-term debt worth 38.67 billion markka would be amortised.
"To ensure sufficient room to manoeuvre in implementing borrowing, net borrowing should be at most 31,000 million markka," the government said.

"The intention is to cover the entire 1997 net borrowing requirement with long-term borrowing, so new state loans with maturities over one-year should amount to at least 69,670 million markka," the government said.
In addition, it would be possible to bring forward repayment of some old foreign debt and it would be good to refinance some markka and currency debt, it added.
"(Therefore) preprations should be made for long-term gross borrowing of a maximum of 77 billion markka in 1997," it said. @
Amortisation of markka-denominated debt in maturities over 12 months would total 20.57 billion markka while foreign currency debt would be amortised for 18.10 billion, it said.

At the end of 1996, the state's short-term debt -- maturities up to 12 months -- was expected to be around 45.0 billion markka, the government said. Currently, outstanding short-term debt in treasury bills is 46.56 billion markka, according to the State Treasury Office.
"For the flexible implementation of debt servicing, the government should be able to let the stock of outstanding short-term debt in 1997 to be at most 55,000 million markka," the government said.
It further requested authorisation to make interest rate and/or currency swap arrangements on 40.0 billion markka worth of state debt for hedging.
By the end of 1997, state debt was expected to rise to 431.6 billion markka or 71.9 percent of GDP from 402.7 billion markka or 70.8 percent projected at the end of this year, the government said.
